paragraphs.text: Aoaz is a continent of thirteen regions, with the Middle Lands at its heart. The regions are the Cold Lands, the West Lands, Triton’s Islands, the North Lands, the Dark Lands, the Middle Lands with Aenor Isle off their west coast, the Magical Lands, Zol’s Mistake, the East Lands, the South Lands, the Ember Lands, the Islands of the South and the Lands of the Sun.

The far west and north of the Cold Lands, and the far east and south beyond the East Lands and the desert of the South Lands, run off the edge of every chart. No chronicle tells what lies beyond them. The lands south of the South Lands, home of devils, demons and other evil beings that live in fire and endless suffering, are known by name only, and no traveller’s chart shows them.

A wide sea parts the West Lands from the Middle Lands, wider than the old charts draw it. It made the first voyages of exploration slow and the supply of the first settlements hard, and it keeps the West Lands’ quarrels with Aenor alive. The charts of this age show the Fourth Age only: the settlements, frontiers and war-roads of the First Age were not the same.

Close on three hundred crowns, dominions, clans and island lordships divide the continent. The greatest are Aenor and its Concord in the Middle Lands, Lerendor in the North Lands, Coldor in the Cold Lands, Noris and Stabilo in the East Lands, Goldoroth and Dondor in the Dark Lands, Volgan in the Ember Lands and Zol’s Mistake in the black north. Aoaz has known peace for more than seventeen centuries.
paragraphs.note: The length of the peace (more than seventeen centuries) follows the proposed Fourth Age chronology.

plate.subject: fields and forests around a great lake

paragraphs.text: The Middle Lands lie at the centre of Aoaz: plains, forests and mountains around the Great Lake. Here stands Aenor, the Middle Kingdom, the central great power of Aoaz, with its seat at Parim. Selen, Kilinti, Kingson, Konori, Hunhun, Herez and the rest of the Concord’s twenty-six dominions keep their own lords around it. The Cursed Lands and the Bloody Forest resist its rule.

The giants’ kingdom of Hirolon is sovereign and treats with Aenor from outside the Concord. Aenor Forest, the largest forest of the Middle Lands, is the home of the Baelim, a walking tree people who are not ents; the ents live in Kilinti, and the two never share a forest. To the east the mountains of the Great Wall of Aenor part the Middle Lands from the Magical Lands, and off the west coast lies Aenor Isle.

Aen ended the War of Men and made the first united kingdom of men, and the realms of the Middle Lands grew from three threads. The first is that war and the peace that Aen spoke over the kneeling kings, which made Aenor. It also left the Orran houses of the downs and the red-oak forest a grudge over the old names of the Vale’s rivers.

The second thread is the centuries of the Necromancer’s Order, which the vale-folk, the ship-houses, the guilds and the Klungori Guard each survived in their own way. The third is the older peoples of the land, the giants, the ents, the Baelim, the gnomes, the dwarves and one elven household, whose roots lie beyond the chronicles of men.

In the First Age Aenor knew centuries of prosperity and settled lands beyond the Middle Lands, until misrule and revolt left it open to Volgan, who took its capital in his war. It rebuilt in the Second Age, and at that age’s end, in 2A 2133, Elzon took it. Men resisted his Order through the Third Age. When he died at last, a good king restored the monarchy, and a long peace followed under the kings of the Fourth Age.

sources.section: The Third Age and restored monarchy

paragraphs.text: Aenor Isle lies off the west coast of the Middle Lands and is counted a part of them. Its realm is Orohaf, the realm of the Isle Houses, which are ruled by their eldest women. Their queen is chosen holding her house’s steering-oar at the turn of the tide, and the Houses give their dead to the tide.
paragraphs.note: That the Houses give their dead to the tide is adopted from the fallen-realm lore (K64).

paragraphs.text: The Isle Houses are the Water clan of the Low Country, the land the sea took long before Aen, and they say their eldest woman steered the last boat through the Night of the Sea. On the isle’s high ground stand the tide-chambers, rock-cut halls that flood at every high water, and the queen is chosen in one of them. The Houses keep this law without knowing why they keep it.
paragraphs.note: The tide-chambers and the law kept without knowing why are adopted from the fallen-realm lore (K64).

paragraphs.text: Orohaf counts among the dominions of the Concord and keeps its own law under the Charters of Parim. West of the isle the sea lies shallow, and the fishers’ nets bring up field-walls and quern-stones from the banks.

sources.section: The Middle Lands: Aenor and the Concord

plate.subject: a caravan on an ice road under a pale sky

paragraphs.text: The Cold Lands are the north-west of Aoaz, its largest landmass and the least known. They run beyond the western and northern edges of every chart, and a broad neck joins them to the West Lands in the south. Their tribes, the yeti of the Yeti Lands, the ice giants of Nivaros and the free towns of the coast live by trade, herding and hunting.

Coldor rules the frozen interior and the western ports and leads the Northern Accord with Horidor. In 4A 850 Coldor’s kings brought the frozen interior under one crown; Melkgard refused, and it has been Coldor’s rival ever since. Goblins shun the deep cold but hold sheltered valleys in the south of the Cold Lands.

Most of the north shares one root: the fall of the Sunfields, the land of the first men of the north-west, when the winters lengthened and the ice came south. Each heir remembers it differently. Coldor’s fire-keepers say the land was punished, and that the fire their forebears carried into the first Long Dark, a red ember in an aurochs horn, is what was spared.

The road-wardens of Horidor still keep the cairns and red-ragged guide-poles their forebears raised over the Neridor Gap for those who walked south. The moor clans of Fearno say that a crown eats first and feeds last. The reindeer clans of Kvittumm say their forebears followed the herds north-west into the ice country and learned from the reindeer how to live there.

Other peoples of the north have other roots: storm-driven crews who swore on a whale’s tusk, goblins who crossed a frozen channel behind a lantern, yeti who answer the Hum, giants who say the snow breathes over the ages. Far in the north, above the small town of Yeldenne, stands the Castle of Yeldenne, the hall of Horos.

plate.subject: green hills crowded with small castles

paragraphs.text: The West Lands lie south of the Cold Lands, joined to them by a broad neck, and snow falls only near the neck. Two dozen kingdoms crowd them, among them Gunwyn, Girdon, Kradlon, Corogon, Varnondor and Lambin, with the hired companies of Buldor. They trade with Aenor across the wide central sea and resent its tariffs.

The West Lands had peoples and kingdoms before Aenor’s ships came. Aenor’s first settlements there provoked wars with those peoples, and the West remembers the settler wars as theft. Every western court remembers that Aenor once tried to rule it. Aenor reached the West only by ship, and the wide sea made its rule hard to hold.

Aenoran merchants returned to the West between 4A 150 and 212, and the western lords accepted the trade but not the old claims. From 4A 1702 the wars of Gunwyn and Girdon divided the West for half a century, until the two signed the Truce of the Grey Ford in 4A 1745. The truce holds, uneasily, and the West is divided and at peace.
paragraphs.note: The rivalry of Gunwyn and Girdon is established; the dates and the truce are proposed.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: The West shares one grievance and differs in everything else. The downs clans came over the neck on foot, and the Erg clans came down the coast by boat. The settler towns broke with Aenor each in its own way. The dwarf holds of the western ranges lost their deep roads, a great plague made the companies of Buldor, and the small folk fed their neighbours through famine.

Triton’s Islands lie west of the West Lands and arc around the Pupor Sea. Adel, Pollos, Raerby, Nondondor and some thirty island lordships live by fishing, piracy and charting. In 4A 702 the islanders charted the Pupor and sold their charts to every crown.

sources.section: Triton's Islands and the Islands of the South

paragraphs.text: The chart-islanders are lean, weathered sailors of their own kind, and their words for reef, strait, cape and tide are older than any chart. Every realm of the arcs keeps one piece of a dead league of the sea or of the first crossings. Adel keeps the lead that proves a reef, Raerby the cut fish of its banks-court, Pollos the three keys of a strong-room, and the Lens the league’s light.

Halenor keeps the shore-fire that guides kin home and strangers onto the rocks, Santon the black sail of the plague ships, and Nondondor a crown twisted from rope. From the first crossings came Fineger’s white ram on the ice, the kites of the Windy Lands and the grey seals of Seite, which no household kills.

Benan’s corsairs hold the Cursed Square, a square of reefs that wrecks ships, and never enter it. The islanders hold that the Square is cursed, and they do not agree whether the sickness called the Grey Breath still waits in its wrecks. What the reef-spirits are is the islanders’ own belief, and no chronicle tells what lies beneath the Square.

plate.subject: sea-green fleets in a narrow strait

paragraphs.text: The North Lands lie north of the Middle Lands across a narrow strait. Lerendor, one crown since Lerendor and Lerendor’s North joined their royal houses in 4A 411, is the strongest power of the North and leads the Leren Compact with Eekedor. Its kings are proud and its fleets guard the strait. The smaller crowns, among them Tolvael, Molot, R’en and Mina, look to Lerendor or to Parim as it suits them.

The North Lands were allies of Aenor and never its subjects. In 4A 512 the Treaty of the Narrow Strait bound the North Lands and Aenor to defend each other across the strait. Since the toll quarrel of 4A 1716, when Lerendor’s envoys were humiliated in Parim, the Leren court has doubted the treaty.
paragraphs.note: The alliance is established; the treaty’s name and the dates are proposed.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: The crowns of the North are almost all Leren, and each keeps one deed or custom no other crown shares: a whale that led the first captains through the shoals, a steelyard that weighed a raider’s sword against grain, marsh stakes moved by night. Dwarves hold the great ranges of the North, and the dwarf goblins, a people of their own, live in the hills near Lerendor.

The dwarf hold of Hrakbrund, under the High Mountains, keeps a sealed door at the head of an old road under the strait. No chronicle tells where the dwarves or the dwarf goblins first came from, who cut the smooth square workings in Mina’s ore hills, or what lies beyond Hrakbrund’s door.

plate.subject: holds on a dark shore by a black-green sea

paragraphs.text: The Dark Lands lie between the North Lands and the Middle Lands, across narrow straits, on the Sea of Darkness. Goldoroth, an orc kingdom, wants the whole region; Dondor, a kingdom of men, leads the Dark Sea Accord against it. Bordon, Dreson, Dulundur, the Troll Forest and a dozen orc and goblin holds belong to nobody.

The Dark Lands were never one realm. Men, orcs, goblins, trolls, ogres, giants and demons live there under separate rulers, and none of them is Volgan’s by nature. Smash, the troll king, rules the trolls of his own forest only. Volgan’s envoys court the holds, and most still answer only to themselves.

Volgan opened dealings with Dark Lands powers in the First Age, and orcs and goblins marched in his armies, while other parts of the Dark Lands joined the Grand Alliance. Dark Lands soldiers fought on both sides in his war. In the Third Age the Necromancer relied on orc and goblin hosts, and the Buried Wars of 3A 431 to 690 wore down his strength.

The roots of these realms are the stories of peoples who were used by masters, left behind by them, or refused them, and each realm’s law grew from the way it met a master. The orcs of the iron hills chant the Long Walk of the clans left on a lost field, and the sea orcs of the isles broke the shackles of the galleys they rowed. In about 4A 1450 orc warlords united the inner Dark Lands as Goldoroth, and its wars with Dondor began.
paragraphs.note: The year of Goldoroth’s rise is proposed.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

plate.subject: a forest of silver and leaf-green light

paragraphs.text: The Magical Lands lie east of the Middle Lands on the same landmass, parted from them by the mountains of the Great Wall of Aenor, and a long rift sea parts them from the East Lands. They hold the Magical Forest, the Mushroom Forest of the mycids, the Magic Mountains, Herrodon, Andos Enda and Nolorim, which guards the high passes.

The elves of the Magical Lands were never conquered, not by Volgan’s corrupted kin and not by Elzon. They helped the Grand Alliance in Volgan’s war and afterwards kept the Elven Refusal. The Magical Forest is the oldest and most peaceful of their realms, ruled by an elected council of houses. Around it lie twenty smaller elven realms, and Herrodon and Andos Enda are old rivals.
paragraphs.note: The council of houses as the Forest’s rule is proposed.

paragraphs.text: The roots of these realms are not stories of empire. Each is one deed, gift, loss or oath from which a small community’s law grew. The council of the Magical Forest speaks only while a house holds a bough that the grove has let fall, and nobody breaks a bough from a living tree. The rule was broken once, when the houses felled the northern wood against the Black Roots in 3A 802.

sources.section: The Magical Forest: the First Listening

paragraphs.text: The elven powers can command the dragons of Dragon Mountain. The rift-coast elves were neighbours of the Bridge Kingdom of the deep past and never its subjects, and the ferry of Luv-zhise still crosses its drowned road. In the Zilin Hills stands the Worshipdom, a temple-state of the Deliverer that holds three valleys and almost no army. Its pilgrim houses feed and doctor a guest before they ask who he is.
paragraphs.note: The Worshipdom as a temple-state of three valleys is proposed.

paragraphs.text: Zol’s Mistake is a vast black region of the north: a barren wasteland and all the black islands of the Kusmeel. It is almost empty of the living and roamed by the dead. It takes its name from Zol, the Old God of Death and the only Old God in Aoaz. No chronicle tells what made the land a Mistake.

Zol came to the black north long before Aen and Volgan, and the land was already desolate. In the First Age his power there lay dormant: its lands gave no armies and no help to anyone, and he took no part in the battle of Dardan. Zol has no body in Aoaz.

The realm is held in the name of Zol, and its seat is Furviatlon. It is not known who keeps Furviatlon. The dead who wander the land have no known allegiance, and the scholars do not agree what they are.

The Mistake has no founder, no first king and no tongue of its own, so the living of the north tell its roots from the sea. The oldest sea-words of the north-west have a word for the black coast that means only the shore from which nothing comes back. On the outer isles someone laid the dead inside rings of black stones, each ring left open on its northern side, and nobody knows whose hand that was.

The Leren fishers who began to winter on the isles in 4A 230 took up the custom, because the dead belong to the Old God of Death and a closed ring would be a theft from him. They leave the first fish on the black shore, keep silence on still nights and never speak a certain name at sea. The winter tales of the north tell of Kusven, the grave-wind.
In 4A 1744 fishermen of the isles told of black ships among the islands of the Kusmeel. Nobody in a royal court believed them.
The dead of the Mistake rose and went out beyond it, and the fishermen’s tales of black ships proved true. These dead were held together by Zol’s own magic, and ordinary weapons could not end them.

sources.section: V. The end of the age, 4A 1748 to 4A 1760

plate.subject: domed cities by a rift sea

paragraphs.text: The East Lands lie across the rift sea in the east and run off the eastern edge of every chart. They are the richest region of Aoaz and the most divided. Noris, with Naamis in the Noris Treaty, and Stabilo, with Drak in the Stabilo Pact, compete for the caravan roads, and Alerhia, Erco, Plutondo and many others are great kingdoms in their own right.

sources.section: The East Lands and the South Lands

paragraphs.text: The great caravan roads of the East opened between 4A 600 and 780. Noris and Stabilo grew rich on them, and the rivalry they began then has never fully ended.

The realms of the East are built on two memories. The older is the Bridge Kingdom, from the days when one Eastern people held both shores before the rift opened. Alerhia’s stair, the pillars of the Delbiz horse-fair, Stabilo’s bronze Measure, Ostoroth’s cedar, Mora’s hot lake and the flood that sent Orato’s families onto their heights all keep it.

The younger memory is the Kalioth Crown of the First Age, which almost every realm of the south and the desert remembers from underneath: Noris’s locked wells, Drak’s broken collars, Plutondo’s glass ploughshares and Erco’s buried diadem. The north coast remembers Volgan’s ship-tax, which made Naamis a crown of harbour-mothers and Woqood a people of refusers.

No chronicle tells what broke the land between the shores, or what became of the Kalioth Crown’s provinces beyond the Melty Pass. The salt-boilers say that something breathes under the Hot Lake, and the scholars do not agree whether they are right.

The South Lands are the great desert of the East Lands, which stretches south beyond the edge of every chart. Its two realms are Miaed of the gorge-houses and Wahatud of the well-clans of the dune sea, and they are built on two kinds of water.

Miaed sells water, to the going and the coming alike. Its gorge-houses found the paths of the Hardtmuth by following the black ibex, which they never hunt. Its pass-lords sold water and guides on the passes to Volgan’s eastern clients and to the host of the Kalioth Crown going north, and sold water again to that host’s starving remnant when it came back.

Wahatud gives water before it asks a name. Its dark-skinned well-clans keep a compact with the sand golems that the oasis-folk believe sleep in the dunes. They keep the tale of the white dune, where a dying clan-mother left her last water for a stranger, and her clan found a spring and a white feather.

Beyond the last well lie the burning lands, home of devils, demons and other evil beings that live in fire and endless suffering. They are known by name only, a name of dread, and no traveller’s chart shows them. Angels too are known in the South, but no chronicle tells their history or their purpose.

The Ember Lands lie south of the Middle Lands and are the chief dominion of Volgan, the Great Spirit and the first of the dark lords. They hold Mirolon, Nan, Khorvrath, Dolon, Nezer and the Nether. Volgan’s seat is Nafeher; the demon realms of Khorvrath, Dolon and Nezer are bound to him in the Southern Dominion, and Mirolon stands against him. Nazerun is the old name of Nezer.

Volgan’s realm holds grave hosts, demons of the Netherborn, orcs, ogres, monster clans and necromantic orders, but his rule does not reach every power of the Dark Lands or every monster of the north. Fierce storms at sea and the heavy heat farther south long kept the explorers of men out of the Ember Lands.

In the latter First Age Volgan invaded Mirolon and made it the opening of his war against Aenor. After his defeat the spirits banished him to the Void, and when the Grand Alliance tried to conquer the Ember Lands, Elzon led the remaining defenders and drove it back. In the Third Age Volgan could not leave the Ember Lands while Elzon ruled Aenor in his name, and the native magic of the Ember Lands sustained the Necromancer.

sources.section: Third Age after the reconquest of Aenor

paragraphs.text: The Nether, seat of the demon king, lies in the south, and the Abyss of Roka lies in the Ember Lands as well; neither is the Void that once held Volgan. The realms here are Puvulan, Volgan’s own realm about the Gate of Nafeher, three demon houses who each carried one craft up out of the Halls beneath the Nether, the court that seals every pact, and the men of the peninsula.

sources.section: The shape of the Ember Lands
Newly confirmed places within the Ember Lands

paragraphs.text: The men of the peninsula take their signs from how they lived beside the Dominion: watching it from the swamps, as Mirolon did, salting their dead against it, fleeing it through the storm belt, or sheltering what escapes from it.

sources.section: The shape of the Ember Lands

paragraphs.text: The Islands of the South lie in two arcs south of the West Lands. Howan, Nara, Verde, Enhis Is Rond and the other island realms are small, poor and hospitable. Aenoran voyages reached them in the First Age, and the island peoples supplied the Grand Alliance in Volgan’s war.
paragraphs.note: That the islands are small, poor and hospitable is proposed.

sources.section: Triton's Islands and the Islands of the South

sources.note: 07 - History/Roots of the Islands of the South.md

paragraphs.text: The islands share the guest-right and the Wave-Tally, which began when the first canoes counted their dead as waves on the reef. Each realm keeps one object of its own way of life that its oldest tale made sacred: a diving stone, an upswept roof, a mangrove, a quenched torch, a cane fish-trap, a hand blown in ochre, a water divider and a slit-drum.

sources.note: 07 - History/Roots of the Islands of the South.md
07 - History/Roots of the Islands of the South.md

paragraphs.text: One shrine of the islands, drowned beneath the tide by the Rising Tide of 2A 40, repeats Aen’s name, and the islanders do not know why. No chronicle tells who carved the name there, or when. Nor does any tell what calls from the Night Reef, or where the first canoes of the Yong villages came from.

sources.note: 07 - History/Roots of the Islands of the South.md
07 - History/Roots of the Islands of the South.md

plate.subject: white-gold towers in hard southern light

paragraphs.text: The Lands of the Sun lie in the far south-west and run beyond the southern edge of every chart. Elvana, Igara, Soyano, Yeni Alang and Tor Luni lie here, by the Sea of Gods. The Sunhot elves, a people far taller than men and among the strongest and most peaceful of Aoaz, live in many small realms led by the Lands of Light.
paragraphs.note: The Lands of Light as leaders of the Sunhot realms is proposed.

paragraphs.text: Among them the Gala elves keep their ancient court under King Lorien, and they are the most powerful of the elves. Lorien led the Gala host in Volgan’s war, and lost many of his people in King Edran’s invasion of the Ember Lands, which he had opposed. Whether the two peoples are kin, no chronicle of men can say.

sources.note: 07 - History/Roots of the Lands of the Sun.md

paragraphs.text: Each realm of the South-West keeps one deed or custom no other shares. Gala keeps a spring and a white hind. The Lands of Light keep the noon-door and the only sun among the banners of the region. The cape keeps a silk-moth, the shallows a crane, the terraces a still ribbon and the quarries a broken chisel.

sources.note: 07 - History/Roots of the Lands of the Sun.md

paragraphs.text: The isles keep a shared canoe and a mother-keel. The Sunfolk of Goodin, men who came as boat-folk, keep the spear reversed as guests do. The forest of the Keepers holds one winged seed and its silence, and the Keepers are forest spirits never fully shaped like men. No chronicle tells who raised the standing stones of Tor Luni, or what lies beyond the south-western sea.

sources.note: 07 - History/Roots of the Lands of the Sun.md
07 - History/Roots of the Lands of the Sun.md

plate.subject: a lake harbour with merchant ships below the palace towers

paragraphs.text: Parim is the seat of Aenor, the Middle Kingdom, on the Great Lake of the Middle Lands. The Golden King has reigned here since 4A 1729. He sells offices, rewards flatterers and spends the treasury on the Golden Court, yet the institutions of seventeen centuries keep the kingdom running.
paragraphs.note: The year of the Golden King’s crowning and the seventeen centuries are proposed.

sources.section: The Middle Lands: Aenor and the Concord

paragraphs.text: In 4A 1, after Elzon’s death, Harion of Selen was crowned at Parim and the monarchy was restored. In 4A 3 the Charters of Parim bound the surviving dominions to the crown as self-governing members of a common defence. Between 4A 40 and 120 the roads, the canals and the ports of the Great Lake were rebuilt.

In 4A 212 the First Concord Council met in Parim, and the dominions and the crown agreed on a common army in war and free roads in peace. The universities of Parim and Selen were founded in 4A 340, and their scholars keep this chronicle. In 4A 1000 Parim celebrated a thousand years of peace before envoys from every region.
In 4A 1733 the Golden Court was completed in Parim: a palace district of gilded halls where offices, titles and charters are bought.
A western army crossed the wide sea and held Parim. The kingdoms of the West Lands, which Aenor had once tried to rule, stood in the crown city of Aen’s kingdom.

sources.section: V. The end of the age, 4A 1748 to 4A 1760

paragraphs.text: Afrit came back to Parim and took the crown city again. From the seat of Aen’s kingdom he claimed kingship over all Aoaz.

sources.section: V. The end of the age, 4A 1748 to 4A 1760

paragraphs.text: Selen is a region and a realm of the Middle Lands within the sphere of Aenor, and one of the dominions of the Concord. It has long been known for its rangers. Its arrangements with the crown at Parim have changed across the ages.

Selen’s roots lie in the War of Men. Three bands broken in that war fled into the Weald in one winter and swore the Quiet Law to the Lord of the Weald, a Wild Spirit whose rank the moots will not discuss. They laid three arrows point-down at the oak that is now the Moot Tree. The Host of Selen bears the three arrows still, and turns their points up when it musters.

Harion of Selen was crowned at Parim in 4A 1, the first king of the restored monarchy. In 4A 340 the university of Selen was founded beside that of Parim, and physicians of the Houses of the First Light teach in both.

plate.subject: a stone wall running over hills toward mountains

paragraphs.text: The Great Wall of Aenor is no wall built by hands but an enormous natural range of mountains. It runs from the Organ Mountains past Lunhrim and around Kingson, and parts the Middle Lands from the Magical Lands. Its passes, valleys and snowlines decide the roads between the two lands, and dwarves hold the range.

sources.section: The Middle Lands: Aenor and the Concord

paragraphs.text: Elzon’s Order held watch-posts in the passes against the Magical Lands, which it never conquered. In 4A 96, by the Accord of the Passes, Harion’s grandson and the elven realms agreed to keep a few passes guarded rather than open every road. The elves wanted their old separation; the kings wanted customs posts on the pass roads and a watch against the dragons of the east.

The vale of Kingson says that Aen set one of his sons to keep a fire at the pass. Under the Order’s ban on fire the watch-families carried the vigil ember from hearth to hearth in iron tongs for nearly twelve centuries, and in 3A 1244 they carried it up to open the forts again.

The Klungori Guard, heirs of the last company of the Unbinding, keep their tower in the range and have sworn not to disband until the last of the Order’s creatures leaves it. Kunhrim, the dwarf hold of the range, keeps a sealed door at the head of an old road.
War came into the range, and a pass of the Great Wall changed hands. The Accord of the Passes, kept since 4A 96, was broken.

Two lands of the Middle Lands reject the crown of Aenor: the Cursed Lands of the grey downs and the Bloody Forest of the red oaks. Neither belongs to the Concord. Both keep the Orran tongue and a law of mothers older than Aenor.
paragraphs.note: That both keep the Orran tongue and the mothers’ law is adopted from the fallen-realm lore (K64).

paragraphs.text: The Veiled of the Cursed Lands keep their law on cords. Every field the sea took from the Low Country was tied in black on the Moot’s cord, and the Last Cord lies in the eldest barrow of the downs. When the Black Roots soured the downs, the Veiled counted them the second land to die of asking.

In the Bloody Forest the Wolf, Bear and Raven clans hung their mothers’ cords in the red oaks, which bleed when they are cut. A war-chief there serves for one war only, and it is the mothers who end the feuds.
The Veiled tell of the drowned land as “the land that was asked for too much”. The giants of Hirolon will say no more of it than that.

Mirolon is a kingdom of men in the Ember Lands, and the one realm of the Ember Lands that stands against Volgan. In the latter First Age Volgan invaded Mirolon and made it the opening of his vast war against Aenor and its allies. After his defeat Mirolon was lost to him.

sources.section: The shape of the Ember Lands

paragraphs.text: The lake-kingdom’s survivors hid for five centuries in the Great Swamp and read Volgan’s patrols by the herons. Hadric hung the crown in the beacon tower, and Mirolon’s sign is a grey heron standing watchful.

In about 4A 1650 Mirolon fortified its northern passes. In 4A 1736 a Mirolonese envoy warned Parim that the Ember Lands were arming. The court laughed: Volgan had been quiet for longer than Aenor had had kings.

sources.section: III. The Kingdom Behind the Throne, 4A 1000 to 4A 1729

paragraphs.text: The elves of Nolorim, the herders of the heights who traded with Mirolon’s shore, remember the night of Volgan’s invasion. Their eldest herder blew the great horn of the heights until its bell split, and the warning came too late. At dawn the families swore that the warning would never come late again.
Volgan retook Mirolon, the kingdom he had first conquered in the First Age and lost after his defeat.

sources.section: V. The end of the age, 4A 1748 to 4A 1760

plate.subject: a red sky over volcanic passes

paragraphs.text: The Nether lies in the south of the Ember Lands and is the seat of the demon king, whom men call the King of Demons. In the Second Age the demon Agon and many other demons were active here, and demons came out through portals to raid Aenor and other lands. How far the demon king’s rule reaches is not known, and no chronicle gives his name.

His pacts bind the living; the souls of the dead remain Zol’s. The Nether is not the Void where Volgan was banished, nor the Abyss of Roka, nor the burning lands south of the South Lands, which are known by name only.

The houses of the Nether cut the Halls beneath Mount Nether and took a king whose seal is burned into every pact. That seal, the one five-pointed figure of Aoaz, stands inside a ring of fire. Whether the demon king commands all the Netherborn, and what he owes to Volgan, the scholars do not agree.
The Abyss lies within the Ember Lands. Roka and the Necklace of the Abyss are bound up with its name. No chronicle tells exactly where it lies, what Roka is, or what powers the necklace holds.

The Abyss is not the Void that imprisoned Volgan, and it is not the Nether in the south, where the demon king has his seat. Whether these places touch one another in any way, the scholars do not agree.

sources.section: Newly confirmed places within the Ember Lands

paragraphs.text: Furviatlon is the seat of Zol’s Mistake, the black realm held in the name of Zol, the Old God of Death. It is not known who keeps Furviatlon, or what kind of being keeps it. Aenor counts the black north its rival.
paragraphs.note: Furviatlon as the seat comes from the working political table.

paragraphs.text: Šodolôro lies within the Mistake. The winter tales of the north say it is the dwelling of Kusven, the grave-wind, who serves the Old God of Death. What Kusven truly is, no chronicle tells.

The realm is held under the broken concentric rings of the Will of Zol. The rings first appear on an Aenoran chart of 1A 470, where a pilot of the northern voyages drew them on flat water beside the name, broken where his pen lifted. To the living the sign means that what dies is owed.

plate.subject: a lone peak with dragons above it

paragraphs.text: Dragon Mountain is where the dragons of Aoaz chiefly come from. The dragons form no country, and the elven powers can command them.

The keepers of Yavieth live under its three spurs. Long before Aen, their tale says, elves fleeing a hard winter sheltered there, and a dragon came among them, spared them and left a shed scale by their fire. Their eldest climbed to give it back, and the dragon would not take it; the bond began with that refused gift.

The keepers take only shed scale, never a dragon’s blood, and keep no lists of names. Without their word no realm of the elven kindred asks a dragon for help. Since the Accord of 4A 96 the kings of Aenor have kept a watch in the passes of the Great Wall against the dragons of the east.
paragraphs.note: The Accord of the Passes of 4A 96 is proposed.

paragraphs.text: Dardan was the decisive battle of the First Age war against Volgan. It claimed millions of lives and left a wasteland behind. There the Grand Alliance defeated Volgan, and other spirits stripped his power and banished him. No map of this age marks it, and the scholars do not agree where it lay.
No chronicle tells how long the battle lasted, or by what rite the spirits bound him.

Every people of Aoaz had its dead on that field. Volgan’s host held corrupted elves, allied men of the east and south, orcs, goblins, demons, devils, monsters, dragons, Great Spirits and Damned Spirits. Against them stood the Grand Alliance: the men of Aenor and the western kingdoms, the elves, the dwarves, the giants, spirits, island peoples and some free forces of the Dark Lands.

sources.section: First Age ethnic and political history

paragraphs.text: The peoples remember their dead. The orc Fire-Speakers chant the Long Walk of the clans who were left on the field when the battle was lost and walked home through hostile country. The chroniclers of the East record that the host of the Kalioth Crown stood with Volgan’s and died there.
paragraphs.note: The Kalioth host’s death on the field is adopted from the fallen-realm lore (K64).

paragraphs.text: After the battle the Alliance’s host broke, and the Ember Lands stayed unconquered. Elzon organised the last defence and threw back the Alliance’s invasion, and the elves’ losses in that failure left a long resentment of Aenor’s king.

plate.subject: a dark castle in deep snow

paragraphs.text: The Castle of Yeldenne stands in the far north of the Cold Lands, in Mp’E, above Yeldenne, an ordinary small town. Its lord is Horos, a Great Spirit and an enormous armoured knight, who has kept his hall through the ages. Beneath the castle lie his halls under the earth.

Horos guards a green crystal of old and holy power, which the chronicles call Glo. It is said to hold part of the power of Glernaen, a true New God of Power and Wisdom. In his throne-hall the crystal shines below the seat of the knight, and he keeps it against every claimant.

The shepherds of Pertolor leave a loaf and a fleece at the start of the Silent Road beyond the town of Yeldenne, as the due of the black-faced ram that once led their lost flock down out of the valley of Mp’E. Nobody of the vale walks on. The people of Mp’E believe that the Watcher in the Hall is a sleeping king of the old north.
paragraphs.note: The Mp’E belief in a sleeping king is adopted from the fallen-realm lore (K64).

paragraphs.text: No chronicle tells who built the castle, how the crystal came into the keeping of Horos, or why it may pass only to one worthy of it.

Horos died in his hall. A crowned stranger from the south came for the crystal and wounded the knight from behind, and fled bleeding when the Man from the Ice struck him. Dying, Horos took the crystal from his chest, for it was his own heart, and placed it in the hands of the Man from the Ice, with his blue sword. Then his form crumbled to dust.
The throne-hall of Yeldenne stands empty, and no knight keeps it.
